offence_severity: Minimum: Life imprisonment, Maximum: Death penalty
number_of_offences: Charged with 3 offences, 3 offences finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution has brought on record adequate material that would prima-facie point towards the guilt of the accused, including details about the manner in which the deceased and Nirma were traced by the accused, acts of reconnaissance, and the manner in which each of the accused participated in the alleged crime.
witness_credibility: The court assessed that one of the prosecution witnesses, Nirma, turned hostile, and in the absence of evidence regarding the circumstances under which she turned hostile, there is a possibility that the respondents-accused may have influenced other witnesses or tampered with the evidence.
bail_history: Bail granted by High Court in cryptic and casual order without considering material aspects of the case; subsequent bail granted to Budharam and Rajendra Bishnoi by High Court in similar manner
trial_duration: FIR lodged on 18 May 2020; chargesheet filed on 19 August 2022; trial judgment not specified; High Court judgments on 14 February 2022 and 02 February 2023; Supreme Court decision on 24 July 2023
legal_representation: Pradeep Chhindra, Rajan Chawla, Advs. for the Appellant; B. S. Rajesh Agrajit, Rajesh Chand, Ms. Jyoti Rana, Ms. Pr iya Nagar, Ms. Meetu Goswami, Siddharth Goswami, D. K. Devesh, Asad Alvi, Ms. Saba A. K. Patel, Hamid Irfan, Milind Kumar, Nishant Bishnoi, Ms. Srishti Prabhakar, Tanay Hegde, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered on 18 May 2020; charge sheet filed on 19 August 2022; trial ongoing
procedural_irregularity: High Court granted bail in cryptic and casual order without considering material aspects of the case and without cogent reasoning
appeal_history: Trial court dismissed bail application; High Court allowed bail applications; Supreme Court set aside High Court judgments and cancelled bail bonds
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the High Court's grant of bail was erroneous and lacked reasoning, as the accused were involved in a serious crime (honour killing) with substantial evidence pointing to their guilt. The High Court failed to consider material aspects of the case, such as the gravity of the allegations, the strength of the evidence, and the potential severity of the punishment if convicted.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court was correct in granting bail, as the accused were entitled to liberty unless there was a justifiable reason to deny it. They contended that the High Court did not need to consider the merits of the case in detail and that the accused had no intention to misuse bail, with no evidence of tampering with witnesses or evading justice.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that while liberty is an important right, courts must consider the seriousness of the accusations, the likelihood of the accused fleeing, the impact on witnesses, and the potential for tampering with evidence when deciding bail. An order granting bail without cogent reasoning is illegal.
precedent_relied_upon: Brijmani Devi vs. Pappu Kumar (2022) 4 SCC 497; Deepak Yadav vs. State of Uttar Pradesh (2022) 8 SCC 559; Gudikanti Narasimhulu vs. Public Prosecutor, High Court of Andhra Pradesh (1978) 1 SCC 240; Prahlad Singh Bhati vs. NCT, Delhi (2001) 4 SCC 280; Anil Kumar Yadav vs. State (NCT of Delhi) (2018) 12 SCC 129; Ram Govind Upadhyay vs. Sudarshan Singh (2002) 3 SCC 598; Prasanta Kumar Sarkar vs. Ashis Chaterjee (2010) 14 SCC 496; Ramesh Bhavan Rathod vs. Vishanbhai Hirabhai Makwana (Koli) (2021) 6 SCC 230; Manoj Kumar Khokhar vs. State of Rajasthan 2022 SCC Online SC 30; Jaibunisha vs. Meharban (2022) 5 SCC 465
other_sentence_order: The appeals were allowed, the High Court's impugned judgments were set aside, and the accused were directed to surrender to jail authorities within two weeks. Their bail bonds were cancelled.
